editorNote: Las Vegas is the center of the personal-computer world this week, and the message from the aisles is unmistakable: IBM compatibility is becoming a market of its own.
morningLine: COMDEX opens, graphical desktops beckon, and home computers crowd the Christmas counter.

lead.headline: At COMDEX, IBM Compatibility Becomes the Winning Bet
lead.dek: The Las Vegas show reveals an industry rapidly reorganizing around the IBM PC standard.
body: Fall COMDEX opened in Las Vegas on November 28 with a floor full of machines, peripherals and promises. Yet beneath the variety ran a common current: makers were increasingly defining their products by whether they could work with the IBM Personal Computer and its growing software world.

The Washington Post put the trend plainly in its report from the show: “IBM Compatibility Grows.” That phrase captures more than a sales pitch. Compatibility offered buyers the prospect of choosing among vendors without abandoning familiar programs, disks and workplace habits, while giving smaller manufacturers a standard around which to build.

The exhibition itself had swollen into what a contemporary Christian Science Monitor report called the biggest computer show of its kind. The official show guide preserved by the Smithsonian records the scale and cast of this crowded marketplace, where add-on boards, printers, storage and software could matter as much as the computer case.

For home-computer shoppers, the same week still looked more fractured and price-conscious. But in business computing, COMDEX made the direction unusually clear: the IBM PC was no longer merely one successful machine. Compatibility with it was becoming the wager on which much of the industry expected to build the rest of the decade.

stories.headline: Windows and Visi On Put the Graphical Desktop in View
body: TIME’s November 28 issue described two software leaders giving computer screens a new look. VisiCorp’s Visi On and Microsoft’s newly announced Windows promised work arranged through graphical panels rather than commands alone.

Microsoft had announced Windows on November 10, and a surviving Fall COMDEX video documents an early demonstration. This was still a preview story: the commercial Windows 1.0 product would not ship until 1985.

The significance on the show floor was expectation. Software houses were asking buyers to imagine the personal computer as a visual workspace, with overlapping tasks and a pointing device changing how programs were selected and managed.

stories.headline: Holiday Buyers Enter a Crowded, Cut-Price Computer Market
body: The Christmas selling season finds home computers stacked against one another on price, software and promises of family usefulness. IBM’s newly introduced PCjr adds the biggest business-computer name to a field already defined by Commodore, Atari and other established home machines.

Low sticker prices may be welcome at the counter, but they also reveal the damage of the long price war. Post-COMDEX reporting suggests vendors expect the steep slide to slow in 1984, leaving shoppers to weigh support and software libraries alongside the bargain.

The PCjr remains more holiday conversation than broadly delivered product this week. Its arrival nevertheless reinforces the market’s central question: can a home machine borrow the authority and compatibility of the office PC without losing the affordability that created the boom?

stories.headline: Electronic Arts Mixes Chess Strategy with Arcade Action
body: Archon: The Light and the Dark turns a chess-like board into a field of direct combat. When opposing pieces meet, the contest moves from strategy to an action arena where reflexes can overturn apparent advantage.

The Free Fall Associates design is one of Electronic Arts’ first published titles and a vivid example of the new publisher’s pitch: computer games presented as authored creative works, packaged for a holiday shelf increasingly rich in experiments.

stories.headline: BYTE Asks Software to Become Easier
body: BYTE’s December issue carries the theme “Easy Software,” matching the week’s fascination with windows, pointers and friendlier screens. Usability is moving from a pleasant extra toward a central competitive claim.

The theme joins the trade-show story to the home counter. Whether the buyer is considering an IBM-compatible office machine or a family computer, the winning system may be the one that asks less ceremony before useful work begins.
